conventions.units: Lengths in metres (max_length_m), weights in kilograms, ages in years, egg diameters in millimetres.
conventions.null: null means no authoritative number was found. A null inside a [min,max] pair means that end of the range is unknown.
conventions.max_length_type: TL = total length, FL = fork length, SL = standard length, shell = shell diameter.
conventions.egg_diameter_mm: Ripe egg (roe grain) diameter. Where a source gives only a mean, min and max are equal and egg_diameter_note says so.
conventions.map_points: Approximate, hand-placed representative points on named rivers, seas and lakes inside the native range. They are display anchors, not survey data.
conventions.field_sources: Each key names the field; the value is a key in source_index. See species_notes.md for conflicts and choices.
conventions.iucn_status: Category and assessment date as given by FishBase (which cites IUCN Red List version 2025-2); publication year and assessment id from the published IUCN citation where found. iucnredlist.org itself refused automated access (HTTP 403).

species.taxonomy_note: FishBase now lists this species as Acipenser huso (genus Huso merged into Acipenser); Huso huso is still the name most used in the caviar trade.
species.native_range: Caspian, Black and Azov Sea basins, migrating up large rivers such as the Volga and Danube to spawn; extirpated from the Adriatic.
species.max_size_note: FishBase's 8 m and 3,200 kg are historical published maxima. The best-documented single fish, a female caught in the Volga estuary in 1827, is given by Guinness World Records as 7.3 m and 1,474 kg. Use the 1827 figures for a conservative label.

cites_appendix.note: All Acipenseriformes not already listed were added to Appendix II effective 1 April 1998.

species.wild_status_note: The US listed beluga as threatened under the Endangered Species Act effective October 2004 and suspended imports of beluga caviar and meat from the Caspian Sea countries effective 30 September 2005.
species.one_fact: Depending on her size, a single female beluga can carry anywhere from 200,000 to 8 million eggs, each about 4 millimeters across.

species.taxonomy_note: FishBase now lists this species as Acipenser dauricus.
species.native_range: Endemic to the Amur River basin on the Russia-China border, from upper tributaries such as the Argun, Shilka and Onon down to the estuary and nearby brackish waters of the Sea of Okhotsk and Sea of Japan.
species.female_maturity_note: NOAA figure, sexes not separated. FishBase female records: 11 to 16 years (middle Amur) and 17 to 23 years (estuary population).
species.egg_diameter_note: No authoritative measurement found; only retailer claims (about 3 to 4 mm).

cites_appendix.note: All Acipenseriformes not already listed were added to Appendix II effective 1 April 1998.

species.wild_status_note: Listed as endangered under the US Endangered Species Act since July 2014; NOAA reports the Lower Amur population fell from about 40,000 fish in the 1990s to 19,100 in 2011.
species.one_fact: Kaluga can reach 5.6 meters and about 1,000 kilograms; after their first year they switch from invertebrates to hunting fish, including young chum salmon.

species.native_range: Endemic to the Amur River system on the Russia-China border.
species.female_maturity_note: USFWS says Amur sturgeon begin reproducing after 9 to 14 years (sexes not separated); FishBase female records fall in the same 9 to 14 range.
species.egg_diameter_note: Range of per-female mean oocyte diameters in 14 wild Amur River females with ripe (stage IV) ovaries; overall mean 3.05 mm.

cites_appendix.note: All Acipenseriformes not already listed were added to Appendix II effective 1 April 1998.

species.wild_status_note: The US Fish and Wildlife Service proposed listing the Amur sturgeon as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in August 2021; a final decision was not confirmed in this research.
species.one_fact: Found only in the Amur River system, the Amur sturgeon occurs in two distinct color forms, one brown and one gray.

species.native_range: Caspian Sea, Black Sea and Sea of Azov basins, with both sea-run and freshwater populations.

cites_appendix.note: All Acipenseriformes not already listed were added to Appendix II effective 1 April 1998.

species.wild_status_note: FishBase notes the species is now mainly propagated through artificial reproduction; the Caspian range states set no commercial sturgeon fishing or wild-caviar export quotas in 2014 and said they would set none for 2015 to 2016.
species.one_fact: Scientists crossed Russian sturgeon eggs with American paddlefish sperm, families that split about 184 million years ago, and 62 to 74 percent of the hybrids survived their first month.

species.native_range: Siberian rivers from the Ob east to the Kolyma, including the Yenisei and Lena, plus Lake Baikal; it lives mainly in fresh water.
species.female_maturity_note: Wild fish, depending on origin; farmed females mature at about 7 years.

cites_appendix.note: All Acipenseriformes not already listed were added to Appendix II effective 1 April 1998.

species.wild_status_note: Once caught by the hundreds of tonnes a year in the Ob, Yenisei and Lena basins, wild stocks have declined from dams, overfishing and pollution.
species.one_fact: In 2016 the Siberian sturgeon was the world's top caviar species, supplying about 31 percent of global caviar production by volume.

species.native_range: Pacific coast of North America from the Gulf of Alaska to central California, spawning in large rivers such as the Sacramento, Columbia and Fraser.
species.female_maturity_note: Females, per Chapman et al. 1996 (citing the White Sturgeon Planning Committee). CDFW gives 10 to 19 years for age at first reproduction in California, sexes combined.

cites_appendix.note: All Acipenseriformes not already listed were added to Appendix II effective 1 April 1998.

species.wild_status_note: California shut its commercial white sturgeon fishery in 1901, commercial caviar fishing is illegal in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, and the species is now a candidate for listing under the California Endangered Species Act.
species.one_fact: White sturgeon are the largest fish found in North American fresh water; historic specimens reached about 6.1 meters (20 feet).

species.native_range: Rivers draining to the Black, Azov and Caspian Seas, and Siberian rivers from the Ob east to the Yenisei.

cites_appendix.note: All Acipenseriformes not already listed were added to Appendix II effective 1 April 1998.

species.wild_status_note: Its migratory (sea-run) populations are now extirpated, though local river populations survive in most of its range.
species.one_fact: FAO calls the sterlet the smallest sturgeon species; stocked sterlet males in Russia's Krasnodar Reservoir matured at only two years old.

species.native_range: Caspian, Black and Azov Sea basins (probably extirpated from the Aegean), ascending rivers to spawn.

cites_appendix.note: All Acipenseriformes not already listed were added to Appendix II effective 1 April 1998.

species.wild_status_note: In the Sea of Azov basin, stellate sturgeon have reproduced only through hatchery stocking since the 1970s.
species.one_fact: Its skin is studded with small star-shaped bony plates, and its long, flattened, upturned snout sets it apart from every other Acipenser species.

species.native_range: Mississippi and Missouri river basins of the central United States, plus the Mobile Bay drainage and the upper Rio Grande.
species.egg_diameter_note: Population means: 2.40 mm (lower Platte River, Nebraska) and 2.58 mm (middle Mississippi River, Illinois).

cites_appendix.note: All Acipenseriformes not already listed were added to Appendix II effective 1 April 1998.

species.wild_status_note: Since October 2010, commercial harvest of shovelnose flesh or roe is prohibited where they overlap endangered pallid sturgeon, for example the entire Missouri River in Missouri.
species.one_fact: Because shovelnose look so much like endangered pallid sturgeon, U.S. law bans commercial fishing for them wherever the two species live together.

species.native_range: Mississippi River basin from southwestern New York to Montana and south to Louisiana, plus Gulf Slope drainages from Mobile Bay to Galveston Bay.

cites_appendix.note: Paddlefish were added to Appendix II in 1992, six years before the rest of the sturgeons.

species.wild_status_note: Wild paddlefish roe is still harvested commercially under state permits in some places, such as Kentucky Lake and Lake Barkley in Kentucky (38-inch minimum size).
species.one_fact: The paddlefish's long snout works as an electrical antenna, sensing the faint electric signals of plankton such as water fleas (Daphnia) that it feeds on.

species.taxonomy_note: In 2022 the bowfin was split in two. Amia calva proper lives from the Pearl River (Louisiana/Mississippi) east; fish west of it, including Louisiana's Atchafalaya Basin where most bowfin caviar is harvested, are now the eyetail bowfin, Amia ocellicauda. The numbers below come from pre-split studies of the combined species.
species.native_range: Eastern North America: Amia calva proper ranges from the Pearl River east through Florida and up the Atlantic coastal plain to Virginia, while the eyetail bowfin covers the Mississippi basin, Great Lakes and Gulf drainages west to Texas.

map_points.label: Atchafalaya Basin, Louisiana (now A. ocellicauda range)

species.egg_diameter_note: Freshly laid eggs, least to greatest diameter; the egg capsule later swells to about twice this size.
species.wild_status_note: Louisiana allows commercial harvest of wild bowfin, mainly for roe, with a 22-inch minimum length and a ban on removing eggs from fish while on the water (rules as reported in 2009).
species.one_fact: Bowfin can breathe air as well as water, letting them survive in warm, stagnant, oxygen-poor backwaters.

species.native_range: Large cold lakes and rivers across most of Canada and the northern United States, including the Great Lakes, New England, central Minnesota and Alaska's Copper and Susitna drainages.
species.female_maturity_note: Ontario study, sexes combined; northern populations mature later (females 7 to 10 or more years).
species.egg_diameter_note: Mean of fertilized, water-hardened eggs from Lakes Michigan and Ontario (SD 0.20 mm); unfertilized roe is somewhat smaller.
species.wild_status_note: Wild-caught: Michigan DNR calls lake whitefish by far the most important commercial fish in the Great Lakes, 88 percent of the value of Michigan's state-licensed catch in 2015.
species.one_fact: Lake whitefish spawn in shallow water in fall and early winter; at a near-freezing 0.5 °C, their eggs take about 140 days to develop.

species.native_range: North Pacific, from Korea and Japan through the Sea of Okhotsk and Bering Sea to Arctic Alaska and south to California.
species.egg_diameter_note: Mean diameter of fertilized eggs (Korea); no sourced range found.
species.wild_status_note: Least Concern globally; wild chum are fished commercially across the North Pacific.
species.one_fact: Chum salmon range more widely than any other Pacific salmon, and like all Pacific salmon they spawn once and then die.

related_species.note: Also sold as salmon roe. FishBase calls it the smallest of the true salmon and notes its roe is valued for caviar, especially in Japan.

species.native_range: Pacific slope of North America from Alaska's Kuskokwim River to southern California, plus Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula; introduced worldwide.
species.female_maturity_note: FAO: usually 3 to 4 years (farmed and wild); FishBase has a female record of 3 to 5 years (Ontario).
species.wild_status_note: Least Concern globally and widely farmed, but on the US West Coast one steelhead population is listed as endangered and ten as threatened under the Endangered Species Act.
species.one_fact: Steelhead and rainbow trout are the same species: steelhead migrate to the ocean, grow larger there, and return to fresh water to spawn.

species.latin_note: No authoritative source names a single tobiko species. Tobiko is roe of flying fish in the genera Cheilopogon and Hirundichthys; in a 2021 DNA survey of Italian sushi, the four-wing flyingfish Hirundichthys affinis was the species most often found (6 of 12 samples), with single samples of H. oxycephalus and H. coromandelensis. Numbers below are for H. affinis except the egg size, which is for H. oxycephalus.
species.native_range: Tropical Atlantic: Guinea to Angola in the east, and from the Gulf Stream off Virginia and the northern Gulf of Mexico through the Caribbean to Brazil in the west.
species.egg_diameter_note: Eggs of Hirundichthys oxycephalus (Kyushu, Japan). A sushi survey describes tobiko grains as 2 mm or less.
species.wild_status_note: Hirundichthys affinis is Least Concern and is the most important commercial fish species of the eastern Caribbean.
species.one_fact: In a DNA survey of sushi sold in Italy, 4 of 12 samples labeled tobiko were actually capelin roe, not flying fish.

species.native_range: Coastal waters of tropical, subtropical and temperate seas worldwide, often entering estuaries, lagoons and rivers.
species.max_size_note: FishBase cites a 12 kg report but flags it as unconfirmed.
species.egg_diameter_note: Spawned eggs. Bottarga is the whole salted, pressed and dried ovary, not loose grains.
species.wild_status_note: Least Concern; most mullet farming still depends on fry collected from the wild.
species.one_fact: Flathead grey mullet have been found in water ranging from fresh to 75 parts per thousand salt, about twice as salty as seawater.

species.bottarga_note: The typical species for tuna bottarga: a peer-reviewed analysis describes salted, dried bluefin (Thunnus thynnus) roe as a seafood characteristic of the Mediterranean.
species.native_range: Atlantic Ocean from Newfoundland to Brazil and from Norway to the Canary Islands, including the Mediterranean; spawns in the Gulf of Mexico and the Mediterranean.
species.max_size_note: 726 kg is ICCAT's official maximum weight (a 427 cm fish from the Gulf of Maine); FishBase lists 684 kg and NOAA says up to 2,000 lb.
species.female_maturity_note: Age at 50 percent maturity: about 4 in the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean, about 8 in the western Atlantic (sexes combined).
species.egg_diameter_note: ICCAT gives eggs of about 1 mm.
species.wild_status_note: Least Concern globally; ICCAT manages it as two stocks, east and west of the 45°W meridian.
species.one_fact: A 15- to 20-year-old female Atlantic bluefin can carry up to 45 million eggs, each only about 1 millimeter across.

species.bottarga_note: Also used for tuna bottarga, but no authoritative source on its share was found; bluefin is the traditionally documented species.
species.native_range: Tropical and subtropical seas worldwide, but absent from the Mediterranean.
species.female_maturity_note: 50 percent of females mature at about 2 years (western Pacific) or a little over 2 (eastern Atlantic); no sourced upper bound.
species.wild_status_note: Least Concern globally; in the Atlantic it is assessed and managed by ICCAT.
species.one_fact: Large yellowfin tuna frequently school with porpoises and gather around floating debris and other objects in the open ocean.

species.native_range: Britain, western Europe and the shores of the Mediterranean and Black Seas; introduced widely, including to California in the 1850s as a source of escargot.
species.lifespan_note: No authoritative figure found; non-authoritative sites say 2 to 5 years.
species.female_maturity_note: Hermaphrodite, so this is age at sexual maturity: about 10 months in South Africa, about 2 years in southern California.
species.egg_diameter_note: About 3 mm (CFIA); UF/IFAS gives about 1/8 inch.

iucn_status.scope_note: Only a European assessment was found.

species.wild_status_note: Not threatened in its native Europe, it is an invasive crop pest elsewhere; it was brought to California in the 1850s for escargot.
species.one_fact: Every garden snail is both male and female; after mating it digs a small nest in the soil and lays about 86 round white eggs.

hybrids.why_farmed: This cross shows better viability and growth than either parent species and has become the most exploited sturgeon for caviar production; it supplied about 13 percent of world caviar in 2016.
hybrids.notes: It is one of the five farmed sturgeons that made up 90 percent of China's sturgeon output in 2010-2012. DNA testing has found a high level of concealed hybridization in caviar sold as pure Amur or kaluga.

hybrids.why_farmed: Soviet hybridization work begun in 1949 aimed to combine the beluga's rapid growth with the sterlet's early maturity, and the bester is cultivated for its high-quality eggs.

hybrids.why_farmed_note: No source specific to farming this cross was found. FAO (1971) lists it among natural sturgeon hybrids and says hybrids in general are farmed for rapid growth, greater viability and earlier maturity.
